title: Superlatives that compete
claim: The formula recurs beyond wealth and sometimes collides: nothing surpasses virtue, yet nothing surpasses apt speech; nothing beats truth, yet not killing is ranked above it; poverty is unmatched pain, yet wealth under a tyrant hurts more. Commentators reconcile the first two, and 323 is a deliberate ranking, so these superlatives need case-by-case reading.
audit_issue: Fails on restraint (32-122 is only a shared formula; restraint is a kind of virtue) and 92-225 is forced. The last sentence overreaches: 323 is an explicit ranking and Parimelazhagar treats it as settling the order, so not every superlative is mere praise.

title: Absolute ethics and the needs of the state
claim: Five rules stated without exception in the Book of Virtue meet specific verses in the Book of Wealth that suspend or limit them: killing, anger, hypocrisy, generosity and purity of mind. The verses do not acknowledge this; Parimelazhagar reconciles some by adding limits such as royal duty and enemies only. The Book of Wealth elsewhere upholds ethics (546, 657).
audit_issue: All five named areas have a sound link, though two links are the same pair. Overstated in three ways: 480 limits generosity rather than reversing it; 'often' for commentators' added limits rests on clear cases at 550 and 829; and Parimelazhagar directs 303 at renunciants, so some rules were not universal for him. Counterevidence against a book-wide pattern: 546 and 657 show the Book of Wealth upholding ethics.

title: Echoes of the earlier books in the Book of Love
claim: A few lover-speakers reuse the earlier books' language against its grain: shame worth dying for is set aside to save life (1132/1017), the body-soul bond called flimsy in 338 becomes the image of union (1122), and honour's ban on following those who slight you is called unavailable to the lovesick (1255/966). These are dramatised speeches and do not overturn the earlier teaching.
audit_issue: Of the four named examples only shame holds. Senses and warrior are contrasts without incompatibility, and backbiting is forced because அலர் is not புறங்கூறல். 'Overturns' is false as a claim about the book: these are dramatised speakers in stated situations, on Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's framing, and do not revise the earlier teaching.

title: Where the man and woman differ
claim: On Parimelazhagar's speaker assignments, the man and woman differ over shame (1132/1163) and memory (1202/1207), and 1137 states the first contrast outright. Manakkudavar assigns some speakers differently, and most other differences in the Book of Love follow union and separation rather than gender.
audit_issue: Only shame and memory hold, and memory's gender contrast fails on Manakkudavar, who gives 1202 to the woman. Evening, night and leaving fail: most contrasts are union against separation, not man against woman, and two links lie outside the Book of Love. Counterevidence: 1251 has the woman's shame break, and the man suffers in 1132 and 1268. 1137, the verse that states the asymmetry outright, is not among the links.

title: Truth defined by what it does
claim: On Parimelazhagar's reading, chapter 30 defines truthfulness by harmlessness of effect and explicitly sets aside mere statement of what happened, though 293 still treats lying as going against what one knows. That definition carries real weight: without it, 297's unbroken not-lying and 292's blameless falsehood would conflict.
audit_issue: The second sentence holds (292-297). 'Not agreement with fact' is Parimelazhagar's explicit gloss on 291, not the verse's wording, and 291 appears only in a forced link, so most links do not test the claim. Counterevidence: 293 still treats lying as going against what one's own heart knows, in the same chapter.

title: Where does understanding come from?
claim: The book names at least three sources of understanding that do not sit easily together: study (396), one's own or fated nature (373) and company (454). Parimelazhagar reconciles study with fate by limiting study's reach to where fate does not oppose it. Separately, it is divided on whether a speaker's standing matters (423, 415, 850).
audit_issue: Only study against fate or innate nature and against company hold. Hearing rests on the wrong 396-416, and poverty's absence has no link in this thread. The two sound links on 423 concern a speaker's credibility, not sources of understanding. Parimelazhagar explicitly reconciles 396 with 373, which the thread does not mention.

title: Does virtue pay? The promise and its escape clauses
claim: The Book of Virtue states the reward of virtue as a rule: aram yields wealth (31), the fair person's wealth does not decay (112), the envious have no gain (135, 170), the one who does no evil meets no ruin (210), and all pain returns on those who caused it (320). The same book then admits the counter-case: 169 calls the prosperity of the crooked and the ruin of the upright things to be pondered (நினைக்கப்படும்), and 332 says great wealth comes and goes like a theatre crowd, with no exception for the virtuous. The book keeps the promise alive by two moves. Verse 117 changes what counts as ruin: the world does not set down as கேடு the low state of one who stays in virtue, which Parimelazhagar narrows to the judgement of the high-minded (உயர்ந்தோர்) and Manakkudavar reads as the world counting such loss with his gains. The commentators supply the other move, past deeds: Parimelazhagar sends the wise to look for a cause in earlier births at 169, and Manakkudavar reads 320's returning pain as pain done in a former time.
limits: This is a claim about chapters 4 to 34 of the Book of Virtue, and the escape clauses at 117 and in the commentaries are not stated by 169 itself, which leaves the puzzle open. The earlier version of this thread also drew in the apportioner verses (63, 377) and the curse at 1062; those are not in this cluster but belong to the same question.
audit_issue: The claim says the commentators supply the past-deeds move, which is true inside chapters 4 to 34, but the Book of Virtue itself makes that move in chapter 38 (ஊழ், e.g. 375, 377), right after this range; a reader should not take the text as silent on it. At 117 Parimelazhagar also adds the implied 'செல்வம் என்று கொள்ளுவர்', so he too reads the low state as counted among gains, not only Manakkudavar.

title: Does character survive poverty?
claim: Two verses say the poor person of character is not lowered: 117 for the fair-minded (the world does not count his தாழ்வு as ruin) and 988 for the one with the firmness called சால்பு (இன்மை இளிவன்று). Verse 752 reports the opposite as fact: everyone scorns the have-nots and honours the rich, which Parimelazhagar sharpens to 'even if they have every good quality', while 841 says the world does not count lack of wealth as lack at all. The poverty chapter then shows character itself giving way: 1044 says poverty produces degrading speech even in the well-born, though 139 called evil speech impossible for those with conduct and 959 made speech the reliable sign of lineage; on Parimelazhagar's reading of 223, the well-born never utter the beggar's 'I have nothing', which 1044 denies. Verse 1047 draws the line the book seems to want: the poverty that estranges even one's mother is அறஞ்சாரா, poverty not joined to virtue, which matches 117's boundary and runs against 521's claim that kin honour old ties even when all is gone.
limits: The reconciliation through அறஞ்சாரா at 1047 is the verse's own qualifier, but Pope drops it and reads the verse of poverty in general; and 752, 841 and 1044 are not qualified by virtue, so the disagreement over whether the world and the person hold up under want remains. The earlier version of this thread noted that இன்மை also names the ascetic's chosen possessionlessness (408, 532), a different condition not covered by this cluster.
audit_issue: 841 does not say the world counts lack of wealth as no lack 'at all': its point is ranking lack of wisdom as the worst lack, and Parimelazhagar glosses that the world does not count other lack as lack of that kind. On Parimelazhagar's reading the degrading words of 1044 are begging ('give to us'), not the தீய speech (harmful lies etc.) that 139 rules out, so the 139 and 959 contrasts are weaker than stated. His note on 1047 also says all kin abandon the poor man because he must take and cannot give, which sharpens rather than softens the clash with 521.

title: Fate and agency: who moves the mover?
claim: Chapter 38 places fate one step behind every human cause: effort and sloth arise from a fate of gain and a fate of loss (371), and fate is stronger than any plan (380). Chapters 61 and 62 treat the same மடி as a thing a person chooses (605, காமக் கலன்) and can depose, after which the faults it brought are gone (609 against 604); they make effort the cause of wealth (616) and house the two goddesses in sloth and labour (617), and 618 blames idleness but not misfortune, a line 371 makes hard to draw if sloth is fate's product. Chapter 62 then both concedes fate and defies it: 619 grants that a thing may fail through fate and keeps the wage of the body's strain for effort, while 620 says the tireless see fate's back. Verse 262 extends the regress to austerity itself, which on Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's reading needs prior-birth தவம் to be undertaken at all; Kalaignar reads it as present self-control and removes the conflict. Parimelazhagar narrows the gap at 620 by saying fate blocks only a few attempts, and 468 adds that effort counts only when made by the right method.
limits: The verses do not acknowledge one another; the reconciliations are the commentators'. 371 is a general claim about the mind, whereas 616 to 620 are addressed to the king, so the Book of Wealth may be stating a working rule rather than a doctrine. The related question of whether foresight shields a person from fate (429, 372, 380) is treated in its own thread.
audit_issue: 605 is a weak witness for choice: காமக் கலன் says the four are desired, but கெடுநீரார் ('those whose nature is to perish') points toward a predisposition, closer to 371 than against it. Parimelazhagar also glosses 609's மடியாண்மை as the தாமத குணம் behind sloth, a disposition rather than a single act. Kalaignar reads ஊழ் in 371 and 380 as இயற்கை நிலை (natural condition), which softens the regress.

title: Can foresight guard against what is coming?
claim: Chapter 43 defines understanding as knowing what will be (427, ஆவது அறிவார்) and promises that those whose understanding guards ahead meet no affliction that shakes them (429). Chapter 38 undercuts both ends of that promise: 380 says fate arrives before any counter-plan one devises, and 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish, which Parimelazhagar reads as happening even to one with every kind of understanding, so the trait 427 treats as fixed is itself at fate's disposal. Chapter 67 quietly adjusts 429: 662 keeps avoiding harm beforehand as the first rule but adds not giving way once it has come, which Parimelazhagar reads as the case of a task spoiled by fate. Manakkudavar meets the conflict at 429 directly, allowing that early guarding softens even what comes from past deeds.
limits: The verses are addressed to different readers (chapter 38 to all, chapters 43 and 67 to the king and his ministers), and 429 says 'no affliction that shakes', not 'no affliction', so a narrow reading leaves room for 662. None of the verses names the other.
audit_issue: Parimelazhagar sets 372 in the chapter's wealth context: the loss-fate is the fate of losing what one holds (கைப்பொருள்). That narrows the claim that understanding is 'at fate's disposal'. Parimelazhagar reads 662's ஊறொரால் as not undertaking acts that will come to grief, not as foreseeing harm. And his gloss on 430 gives understanding the work of rebuilding once fate has destroyed, which is the book's own reconciliation of chapters 38 and 43.

title: Which life stands highest: the household or renunciation?
claim: The Book of Virtue awards the first place twice. Chapter 3 says the texts' settled view sets the renouncer's greatness above every other excellence (21) and that those who have discerned the two states and taken on அறம் here stand highest in the world (23), and chapters 27 and 35 divide humanity into those who do தவம் or renounce completely and 'the rest', who are caught in desire or in the net (266, 348). Chapter 5 answers in the same register: the householder who lives by virtue gains nothing by going to the outside way (46), stands first among all who strive (47), has more endurance than those who do penance (48), and his life is the thing the word அறம் names (49). Both Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read 46's புறத்தாறு as renunciation, so the collision between 46 and 342/348 is in the commentaries, not only in Pope; Parimelazhagar fits the two chapters together as a ladder (fame and heaven for householders in 50, release for full renouncers in 348), and reads 49's 'அஃதும் ... நன்று' as granting renunciation parity with the household.
limits: The conflict softens on some readings: Manakkudavar takes 47's முயல்வார் as those who strive for wealth, so 47 does not rank the householder above ascetics, and he reads the 'அஃதும்' of 49 as the household life itself (good if the wife is not blameworthy), not as renunciation. Kalaignar reads 23 as choosing good over bad in general. The thread does not claim the Kural contradicts itself knowingly; it claims each chapter speaks in superlatives for its own subject and leaves the ranking to the commentators.
audit_issue: The claim misreports Parimelazhagar on 46 and 47. He glosses புறத்தாறு as 'இல்லை விட்டு வனத்துச் செல்லும் நிலை', the forest-dweller stage, and takes 47's முயல்வார் as those in the third stage, explicitly leaving out the full renouncers (முற்றத் துறந்தவர் விட்டமையின்). That is how he avoids the collision with 348, so the conflict between 46 and 342/348 rests on Manakkudavar's தவம் and on Pope, not on both commentators. The 23-46 link note concedes this, and the claim contradicts it.

title: Renunciation rests on those who have not renounced
claim: The Kural says the ascetic's state is sustained by people who keep what he gives up. Having nothing is the nature of the vow (344), yet those who say 'we have given up what is desired' have no standing if the ploughmen fold their hands (1036), and 263 assumes that 'the others' hold possessions in order to provide for renouncers (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). On who ranks higher, the book splits by chapter: the chapters on the household and on giving grant the ascetic his own virtue of endurance and award more of it to the provider (48: நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து; 225: enduring hunger comes behind removing it), while 263, on both Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's reading, concludes that தவம் exceeds giving (Manakkudavar: தானத்தினும் தவம் மிகுதியுடைத்து).
limits: 263 is phrased as a question (மறந்தார்கொல்) and its ranking of தவம் over giving is the commentators' inference, not the verse's statement. 1036 is in the Book of Wealth and praises farmers; its point about ascetics is incidental. The thread claims a dependence the book notes, not a doctrine it argues.
audit_issue: Kalaignar reads 263 as a warning that the others should not forget their own austerity while helping renouncers, so the dependence and the ranking both rest on the Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar construal of மற்றையவர்கள் as householders who give in place of doing தவம். 344 states the vow's possessionlessness but says nothing about who sustains it; the dependence is carried by 263 and 1036 alone.

title: Which wealth is the true wealth?
claim: Four chapters crown a different thing as the wealth among wealths or the excellent wealth: grace (241, அருட்செல்வம் செல்வத்துள் செல்வம்), not wanting (363, விழுச்செல்வம்), learning (400, கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம்) and hearing (411, செவிச்செல்வம் ... செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை), while 751 says nothing but wealth is wealth (பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள்). Each verse argues against material wealth by a different defect: 241 by who can hold it (even the base have it), 400 by whether it can be lost (Parimelazhagar: heirs, thieves, the strong and kings cannot take learning), 411 on Parimelazhagar's reading by its impermanence and painful fruit, and 363 by having nothing above it in either world. The form is the same and the winners and the reasons differ, which suggests a rhetorical figure that each chapter fills for its own subject rather than a single ranking. 751 inverts the move: the fact that wealth is found among the base, which 241 counts against it, is exactly the power 751 counts in its favour.
limits: The verses do not rank the crowned wealths against one another; 400 and 411 sit in adjacent chapters and neither mentions the other. 751 is in the Book of Wealth and speaks of standing in the world, not of the goods the Book of Virtue values, so its absolute is in a different register. No commentator treats these as a contradiction.
audit_issue: The figure has further instances the claim does not count, notably 592 (உள்ளம் உடைமை உடைமை, with material wealth நில்லாது நீங்கி விடும, an impermanence argument) and the child as wealth in 63; these strengthen the 'rhetorical figure' reading. The reasons attributed to 400 and 411 are Parimelazhagar's, as the claim says; the verses themselves give no reason beyond கேடில் in 400.

title: Wealth gives everything, on conditions the chapter does not state
claim: Chapter 76 makes large claims for wealth: nothing else makes persons of no account into persons of account (751), grace itself is a child nursed by wealth (757), and those who have made bright wealth in full have virtue and pleasure together for the asking (760, ஒண்பொருள் ... ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு). The conditions come from inside the same chapter and from later ones. 754 requires wealth that came by right means and without wrong, 755 tells one to let go wealth that does not come with grace and love, 1009 uses 760's own word ஒண்பொருள் for wealth amassed by setting love aside and ignoring virtue and says others will take it, and 1002 names nearly 751's thought, பொருளானாம் எல்லாம், as the miser's delusion when it leads to not giving. 973, on Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's reading of the high and low seats as wealth and poverty, limits 751 further: wealth gets a person regarded without making them great. Read together, chapter 76's promises hold for wealth rightly earned and spent, and the book supplies that limit elsewhere rather than in the promising verses.
limits: Parimelazhagar reads chapter 76 as the king's revenue (754's தீது as tyranny, 755's grace and love as the one-sixth tax), so on his reading 751-760 and the private miser of 1002 and 1009 concern different agents. 757's dependence of grace on wealth is not withdrawn anywhere; 755 only conditions which wealth may nurse it. The thread does not claim the Kural disparages wealth.
audit_issue: The title says the chapter does not state the conditions, but the claim itself draws them from 754 and 755 inside chapter 76, and on Parimelazhagar (and Pope's 'honestly acquired') 760's ஒண்பொருள் already means rightly earned wealth, so the 'promising verses' are not unconditioned. In 1002 Parimelazhagar takes பொருளானாம் எல்லாம் as correct knowledge (என்றறிந்து) and makes the delusion the later clinging, so 1002 grants 751's premise rather than limiting it.

title: Asking: praised in one chapter, refused in the next
claim: Chapter 106 (இரவு) and chapter 107 (இரவச்சம்) judge the same act from opposite sides, and the difference is not explained by who the giver is. Chapter 106 praises asking only under a condition on the giver: those worth asking (1051), a gift that comes without pain (1052), a heart without concealment that knows what is due (1053), one who would not conceal even in a dream (1054), where asking is itself 'like giving' (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும்). Chapter 107 takes exactly those best givers, who give gladly without concealing and are dear as eyes, and says not asking is worth a crore more (1061); 1066 then says no purpose, not even water for a dying cow, lifts the disgrace from the tongue. 1066 repeats the move of 222 in the Book of Virtue, which calls taking bad 'even if it were called a good path' (நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது): both verses refuse the best case that could be made for receiving. Parimelazhagar narrows the gap by reading chapter 106 as addressed to the destitute (நல்கூர்ந்தார்) and by glossing 1054's 'like giving' as merely not losing the honour one already has; on his reading even the best asking is neutral toward honour, never a gain.
limits: The verses themselves state no such restriction; the reconciliation is the commentator's. 1052 speaks of pleasure and 1066 of disgrace, so they conflict only if a disgraceful act cannot also be a pleasant one. Kalaignar reads கொளல் in 222 as taking goods by any fair means, which would make 222 broader than begging. This thread covers asking; the valuation of giving for itself (chapters 22-23) is not argued here beyond 222.
audit_issue: Chapter 106 already partly frames asking as a survival exception: Parimelazhagar on 1055 says those who ask by standing silently do so to preserve life and would otherwise die rather than lose honour, so the chapter's praise is less unconditional than the claim's opening suggests.

title: Standing before another: when is the humble posture honourable?
claim: The book uses one posture, standing in want before someone (முன் நின்று, பின் சென்று நிலை), and awards it opposite values according to what is sought and before whom one stands. For learning the posture is honoured: on Parimelazhagar's and Kalaignar's reading of 395, those who learned while yearning 'like the poor before the rich' (உடையார்முன் இல்லார்போல் ஏக்கற்றும்) are foremost and those who would not stoop are lowest (கடையர்); 403 makes the unlearned 'very good' if they stay silent before the learned. For goods the same posture is degrading (1066), except that 1053 allows 'a certain beauty' in standing before a giver of unconcealing heart. 966 names the bad case exactly: standing behind those who scorn you (இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று நிலை) wins neither fame nor heaven. 729 turns the ranking word of 395 around: the one who learned yet fears the assembly of the good is lower than the unlearned (கல்லாதவரின் கடை), so the deference praised in 395 and 403 is right only for the one with nothing yet to say. The Book of Love then puts the honour of 966 out of reach: the dignity of not following one who has turned away is 'not something the lovesick know' (1255), and in 1298 the heart argues from honour the other way, that to scorn him would itself be the disgrace (எள்ளின் இளிவாம்).
limits: Pope reads 395 as the unlearned standing before the learned, not the learner before the teacher; the honour-of-learning point depends on the Tamil commentators' construal of ஏக்கற்றும் கற்றார். 1255 and 1298 are dramatised speeches, not teaching, and 1255-966 is also read in thread:love_overturns. The verses never state the rule 'judge the posture by its object'; it is the pattern of the cases.
audit_issue: The 'one posture' is the writer's construct. 403 and 729 are about speaking or staying silent in an assembly, and 1066 is about asking; none of the three is standing in want before someone. The inference that the deference of 395 is right 'only for the one with nothing yet to say' misreads 395: its learners stand before a teacher in order to learn, not because they are silent. In 1255 Parimelazhagar takes பின் செல்லல் as thinking of him without pause, not physically following.

title: The sulk: love's fruit, but only in measure and only if union follows
claim: The last three chapters of the book treat the lovers' sulk (ஊடல்) as a good, and then fence it on three sides. 1109 lists sulk, making-up and union together as the fruit of love; 1326 ranks the sulk above union, as digesting is sweeter than eating; the book's final verse, 1330, calls the sulk love's pleasure. But 1330 adds the condition 'if they get to come together and embrace' (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்), so the sulk's sweetness rests on the union 1326 placed beneath it. 1302 gives the measure: salt in proportion, and a little too long is a little too much; 1307 names the pain inside the sulk, the fear that union will be delayed; 1304 shows the failed case, leaving the sulker unreconciled is cutting a withered creeper at the root. 1282 states the limit from the other direction: when love is full to a palmyra's measure, not a millet of sulking is wanted. Parimelazhagar reads the whole sequence through அளவு, measure: already at 1109 he glosses உணர்தல் as leaving the sulk 'knowing its measure', and at 1330 he makes the embrace depend on ending the sulk between one too ripe and one too young. 1329 and 1307, both the man's on his assignment, show the same delay feared in the moment and wished for afterwards.
limits: Parimelazhagar reads 1304 as the wife telling the man to go reconcile his courtesans, a taunt rather than a rule, so its use as the sulk's failed case follows Kalaignar's plain reading. He also reads 1282 as the woman's own haste dressed as general advice, not a doctrine. The chapters do not say which of 1326 and 1330 is the final word; they stand side by side.
audit_issue: The claim reads 1307 as fear that union will be delayed, but Parimelazhagar glosses புணர்வது நீடுவது அன்றுகொல் as worry about whether the sweet union will last long (நீட்டிக்குமோ நீட்டியாதோ), and Kalaignar agrees. On that reading 1329's wish that the night be long (நீடுக) matches 1307's worry, so the 'feared then desired' contrast depends on a reading the claim does not name. The claim's sentence 'both the man's on his assignment' is also garbled.

title: Fear: the mark of the excellent and the conduct of the base
claim: The book awards fear and fearlessness to opposite ranks of people. Fearlessness (அஞ்சாமை) is one of the four things a king must never lack (382), yet not fearing what should be feared is folly and fearing it is the work of the knowing (அறிவார் தொழில், 428), and the excellent fear evil deeds that the practised wrongdoer does not (201). At the other end, fear is the whole of the base person's good conduct (அச்சமே கீழ்களது ஆசாரம், 1075), the only check on a freedom 1073 compares to the gods'. Taken together, the verses make fear itself morally neutral: what ranks a person is its object. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both notice the collision at 428 and resolve it the same way, saying that since fearlessness was called a king's excellence, 428 names the things that must be feared (sin, blame, ruin), while Parimelazhagar reads 1075's fear as fear of the king's punishment.
limits: This does not claim the book has one doctrine of fear; the reconciliation by object is the commentators', and 382 and 1075 do not themselves say what is or is not feared. 201's 'fear' is of a sin-induced intoxication on Parimelazhagar's reading, which is further from 1075 than the shared word suggests.
audit_issue: 1075 does not make fear the whole of the base person's conduct or the only check on 1073's freedom: its second half (எச்சம் அவாவுண்டேல் உண்டாம் சிறிது) names desire for gain as a second motive, and Parimelazhagar glosses it as mostly fear, sometimes gain. Manakkudavar on 428 notices the tension with fearlessness (மேல் அஞ்சாமை வேண்டு மென்றாராயினும்) but does not list sin, blame and ruin; that list is Parimelazhagar's alone.

title: Does a fort cure fear, or does fear cancel a fort?
claim: Three verses in the Book of Wealth tie fortification and fear together in a loop. A fort is of value to those who, afraid, look to their own safety (அஞ்சித் தற்போற்றுபவர்க்கும் பொருள், 741); a king who has made no defence will be seized by fear when war comes and quickly perish (569); yet the fearful have no fort at all (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை, 534). Read together they make the fort necessary but not sufficient: its absence produces fear, but fear in the mind makes it useless, which is how Parimelazhagar reads 534 (forests and hills give no profit to a frightened mind). This also gives the kingly fearlessness of 382 a material condition, since 569 shows even a king coming to fear without preparation.
limits: 534's fort is a simile for the heedless losing their wealth, so its first half is not primarily a claim about statecraft; and 741's 'afraid' is, on Parimelazhagar's reading, the weaker party prudently taking refuge, not the cowardice 534 condemns. The loop is a reader's construction across chapters 54, 57 and 75, not something any verse states.
audit_issue: The extension to 382 is the reader's inference: 569 says a king without சிறை comes to fear, but nothing in 382 or 569 makes fearlessness depend on defences.

title: Bowing: good for all, yet shameful in some
claim: The book commends பணிதல் without restriction in three places: bowing is good for everyone and a further wealth for the rich (125), whoever wants a lineage must be humble toward all (யார்க்கும் பணிவு, 960), and greatness always bows while smallness admires itself (978). Other verses then draw lines the general rule does not. 963 makes bowing the duty of abundance and standing tall the duty of want; 903 names a bowing that brings lasting shame, stooping before one's wife; and the honour chapter prefers being called ruined to living by following those who slight you (967), while 680 reports that rulers of small domains do bow to the great and take terms. Read together, the praised humility is the absence of pride in those who could be proud (Parimelazhagar glosses 125 and 978 by பெருமிதம் and தருக்கு), and bowing from fear or for a living is a different act the book does not praise: Parimelazhagar says of 680 that bowing is not the wish of the honourable, so the verse says 'they will accept' as worldly practice.
limits: The unifying distinction between humility and submission is the commentators' more than the text's; Parimelazhagar reads 978's என்றும் as 'even when distinction has come', which removes its tension with 963, and Manakkudavar takes 680 as plain prescription for the weak, not a reluctant report. 963's 'reduced circumstances' is poverty on both commentators' readings, so its clash with 680 holds only if personal honour extends to statecraft.
audit_issue: Parimelazhagar restricts 960's யார்க்கும் to those who deserve reverence (பணியப்படுவார் யாவர் மாட்டும்), so 'without restriction' holds only on the plain text there as well as at 978. The 680 and 967 links bear on the claim only indirectly.

title: Birth: cause of conduct, or its name?
claim: The Kural's verses on lineage (குடி, பிறப்பு) pull in two directions. 951 and 952 make birth the source of conduct: integrity and shame are natural (இயல்பாக) only to the well-born, who do not slip in conduct, truth and shame; 502 and 793 treat family as a criterion to check before trusting a minister or making a friend, and 992 names birth as one of courtesy's two sources. 133 reverses the direction: having conduct is itself குடிமை, and a lapse becomes low birth, so that by 133 whoever slips has already left the class 952 describes; 958 sits between, where a lapse in affection makes people doubt a man's birth but leaves birth as the underlying fact; and 972 denies that birth settles distinction at all, leaving only deeds. The commentators divide along the same line: Parimelazhagar keeps 133 within varna (conduct raises or lowers one's standing within the rank one is born to) and reads 951 as saying the well-born need no teaching, while Kalaignar reads 951 and 952 backwards, as tests by which the well-born are recognised, which aligns them with 133 and 972.
limits: This does not claim the book rejects birth: most verses here (502, 793, 951, 952, 958, 992) treat it as real and informative, and only 972 denies it outright. Nor does 133 abolish the vocabulary of birth; it redefines it, and on Parimelazhagar's reading does so only within a fixed scheme of varna.
audit_issue: Parimelazhagar reads 972's எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் as all human lives (மக்களுயிர்) and its சிறப்பு as greatness or smallness from deeds, so 972 levels birth without naming lineage. Kalaignar also reads 502 backwards, as a test by which the well-born are recognised, which the claim does not mention.

title: வலியார் and மெலியார்: one pair of words, three kinds of advice
claim: The book gives opposite advice about the stronger and the weaker in the same words. In the Book of Virtue, 250 tells one who moves against the weaker (மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து) to remember standing before the stronger, and 302 says anger is bad where it cannot take effect and worst where it can, which Parimelazhagar glosses as anger against the stronger and the weaker. In the Book of Wealth, 861 tells a ruler to avoid opposing the stronger and to want enmity with the weaker without holding back (ஓம்பா மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை), and the warrior's song in 771-772 prefers the spear that missed an elephant to the arrow that hit a hare, which Manakkudavar reads as sending the weak away to fight those who can resist. 493 adds that strength is not fixed: the weaker side wins if it knows the ground and guards itself. Parimelazhagar separates the audiences, taking chapter 31 as addressed to ascetics and 861 to a king; Kalaignar instead rewrites 861 as a wish to fight the strong, which removes the conflict by changing the verse.
limits: The conflict depends on reading 250 and 302 as rules for everyone; if chapter 31 addresses ascetics, as Parimelazhagar holds, the Book of Virtue and 861 speak to different people. 772 is a warrior's boast, not a counsel of policy, and 772 and 861 both favour fighting only when read as rules for choosing an opponent. This thread is a sibling of ethics_vs_statecraft, with its own verses.
audit_issue: The title's 'same words' holds only for 250 and 861. 302's stronger and weaker are Parimelazhagar's gloss on செல்லா இடம் and செல்லிடம், and 772 uses neither word. Parimelazhagar's gloss on 861 counts allies and sound counsel within strength, which makes வலியார் and மெலியார் a reckoning of resources. 773, beside 772 in the same chapter, praises helping an enemy who has fallen, which counts against reading chapter 78 as a mere wish to fight.

title: Enmity: chosen, bought, and refused
claim: Chapter 87 (பகைமாட்சி) treats enmity as a thing to be chosen and kept: 861 tells the ruler to want enmity with the weaker, and 867 says the enmity of one who stays close and acts unfittingly must be acquired even at a price (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் மன்ற). The next chapter opens, in 871, by calling enmity a thing without பண்பு that no one should want even in jest. 995 then says those who know how others feel keep பண்பு even inside enmity, so the quality enmity is said to lack can survive within it. The commentators settle 871 differently: Parimelazhagar narrows it to unworthy enmity (மாணாத பகை), which leaves room for 861 and 867, while Manakkudavar takes it as saying that taking up enmity is bad everywhere (எவ்விடத்தும் பகைகோடல் தீது).
limits: The verses themselves do not distinguish worthy from unworthy enmity; that distinction is Parimelazhagar's. 995 is about conduct toward an enemy one already has and does not say whether enmity should be sought, so it qualifies 871's wording rather than contradicting 871's advice.
audit_issue: Only two links carry the claim. The 995 step trades on a shift in பண்பு: in 871 பண்பிலது means 'yielding no good' (Parimelazhagar: தீமை பயப்பது), while 995's பண்பு means courteous qualities. Saying the 'quality enmity is said to lack' survives inside it is wordplay, not the same quality. Also, neither commentator reads 867's அடுத்திருந்து as 'staying close': Parimelazhagar takes it as having begun a work, and Kalaignar reads 861 the opposite way (fight the strong).

title: Can one virtue stand for all of them?
claim: Verse 33 asks for virtue to be done without pause wherever it can reach (ஓவாதே ... எல்லாம் செயல்). Two later verses each let a single virtue stand for the whole, and they pick different ones: 297 says that if one keeps up not lying, leaving the other virtues undone is good (அறம்பிற செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று), and 321 answers the question 'what is virtuous action?' with not killing, since killing brings every other sin; 323 then ranks the two with not killing first. Whether 297 is really a claim of sufficiency is a dispute the commentators settle differently: Parimelazhagar reads it as advice to hold one virtue unfailingly rather than take on many and fail in some, and records that others construe it the other way; Manakkudavar is one of them, reading it as 'only if one keeps not-lying unbroken is doing other virtues good, otherwise harmful', on which 297 states a precondition, not a sufficiency, and the tension with 33 and 321 largely dissolves. Even the one virtue 297 singles out carries an exception, since 292 counts a falsehood yielding faultless good as truth, so its 'unbroken' not-lying is unbroken only under chapter 30's definition of truth by effect.
limits: This does not claim the book is incoherent: 323 is a deliberate ranking within the chapter, and on Parimelazhagar's reading of 321 அறவினை names the whole class of virtues rather than one deed. The superlative form of 300 and 323 is treated in thread:competing_supremes; this thread concerns sufficiency, not superlatives.
audit_issue: The commentary already raises this conflict itself: Parimelazhagar on 323 says the ranking was given because 297 and 300 had left in doubt which of the two virtues is higher. He also says of both 297 and 321 that the one virtue yields the fruit of all the others, which strengthens the sufficiency reading the claim treats as disputed.

title: Can a good result excuse the breach?
claim: The Book of Virtue answers this differently for speech and for gain. For speech, 292 says yes: a falsehood that yields faultless good (புரைதீர்ந்த நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்) belongs with truth, and this is what keeps 297's unbroken not-lying consistent with it. For gain, 113 says no: gain got by leaving fairness is to be dropped that very day even if it brings nothing but good (நன்றே தரினும்), while 177, three chapters later, refuses covetous gain by arguing from its outcome, that its fruit is not good when enjoyed, an argument 113's concession makes unnecessary. Parimelazhagar narrows the gap from both sides: on 113 he takes நன்றே தரினும் as a concession made for the sake of argument, since such gain in fact yields no good, and on 292 the good that licenses falsehood is itself அறம், such as saving a life from ruin or death; for him the outcome that counts is harm or benefit to others, never advantage to oneself.
limits: 113 concerns wealth and 292 speech, and 292's புரைதீர்ந்த (free of fault) may already exclude the gain 113 forbids, so the verses are not a flat contradiction. The internal logic of chapter 30 is covered by thread:truth_by_effect; this thread adds the comparison with the treatment of gain.
audit_issue: Chapter 12 itself argues gain from outcome as well (116: கெடுவல்யான் என்பது அறிக ... நடுவொரீஇ அல்ல செயின்), and Parimelazhagar sums up 112 and 113 as fair wealth yielding good and the other yielding evil, so the contrast between outcome-free 113 and outcome-based 177 holds only on 113's literal concession.

title: Trust once given, and the watching that goes on
claim: Chapter 51 ends by forbidding two errors, trusting one not examined and doubting one examined and trusted (510, தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு), after 501 has set out the fourfold test, and 517 draws the practical conclusion: having reasoned who will finish what by what means, leave the work with him (அவன்கண் விடல்). The next chapter and chapter 59 pull the other way: 514 says many who passed every test change through the nature of the work itself (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும் மாந்தர் பலர்), 520 tells the king to look into the one doing the work every day (நாடோறும் நாடுக), and 584 makes the king's own officers the first object of the spy's inquiry. Testing before appointment therefore does not end examination, and the book's rule against doubt has to coexist with daily inspection. The commentators reconcile them by distinguishing watching from visible suspicion: Parimelazhagar on 510 says the forbidden doubt is suspicion without a fault found, which the man notices and which slackens his work and invites enemies to detach him; on 520 the daily inquiry is to be made within the king himself so that the man's standing (உரிமை) is not destroyed; on 514 he recommends a middle-sized task to expose those who change after appointment. Manakkudavar reads 514 as a warning not to grow careless because one has already trusted.
limits: The verses themselves never say the inspection must be private; that is the commentators' addition. 584's spy examines kin and enemies as well as officers, so spying may be routine inquiry rather than the particular suspicion 510 forbids, and 520-510 is a tension only on the stricter reading.
audit_issue: 584 lists வினைசெய்வார் first but gives no priority among the three groups. Manakkudavar takes 517 as aimed mainly at the army commander.

title: Does remembering the beloved comfort or burn?
claim: Chapter 121, the lament of those who remember, holds two opposite accounts of memory. 1201 and 1202, which Parimelazhagar gives to the man, make recollection a joy that does not fade even in thought (உள்ளினும் தீராப் பெருமகிழ்) and say no pain comes from thinking of the one you love. 1207, 1209 and 1296, spoken by the woman, make the same act the wound: even remembering burns her heart (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்), thinking hard on his lack of tenderness (அளியின்மை ஆற்ற நினைந்து) wastes her life, and thinking alone leaves her heart there only to eat her. The verses together locate the difference in what is remembered: Parimelazhagar glosses the object in 1201-1202 as the pleasure of past union and in 1209 and 1296 as his neglect and cruelties, and Manakkudavar reads 1202 as conditional, sweet only if no pain comes from the thinking. 1215 adds that for the woman even the sweetness of seeing him, awake or in a dream, lasts only for the moment of seeing, where the man's persists in thought.
limits: These are dramatised speeches in different moods, not a doctrine the book states and then retracts. The gender contrast rests on Parimelazhagar's speaker assignments; Manakkudavar gives 1202 to the woman, which keeps the condition but dissolves the contrast. The 1202/1207 pair is already cited in thread:gender_asymmetry, which this thread does not replace since it treats memory rather than gender.
audit_issue: 1296 is in chapter 130, not 121. Parimelazhagar takes the object remembered in 1207 to be the same past pleasure as in 1201 (அவ்வின்பத்தை மறத்தலறியேன்) and says separation burns despite the memory, so 1207 does not fit the claim's resolution by 'what is remembered'. On 1215 the 'only for the moment' reading is Manakkudavar's (அப்பொழுதைக்கு இன்பமாம்); Parimelazhagar reads the verse as saying waking and dream are equal for her, and the contrast with the man's lasting joy is the writer's construction.

title: Who may call him cruel?
claim: In separation the woman's body is read as public testimony, and the verses dispute what it testifies to and whether she wants it heard. In 1188 she complains that the town says only that she has grown pale and no one says he has left her. Yet in 1190 she calls the name of pallor good provided people do not broadcast his unkindness (நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்), and in 1236 what hurts her, more than her slackening bangles and shoulders, is hearing him called cruel (கொடியர் எனக்கூறல் நொந்து). The friend reads the same body the other way: in 1232 the pale weeping eyes seem to tell of the lover's unkindness, and in 1235 the wasted shoulders declare the cruelty of the cruel one; both commentators frame 1232, 1235 as the friend's blaming of the man to console her (இயற்பழித்தல்), and 1190, 1236 as her refusals. The asymmetry is exact: she herself uses கொடியார் கொடுமை of him in 1169, where the long nights outdo his cruelty, but will not accept the word from another mouth.
limits: This is a consistency in one dramatised speaker across chapters 117, 119 and 124, not a teaching stated by the book. 1188 has no aligned commentary in the corpus, so its speaker is inferred from context; and 1169 is tied to 1235 by shared phrasing alone, so its weight in the thread is the word she uses, not a link of argument.
audit_issue: The claim that 'both commentators frame 1232, 1235 as the friend's blaming of the man (இயற்பழித்தல்)' is wrong for 1232. Manakkudavar has the friend warn that the tears are becoming gossip so that she will bear up, and Parimelazhagar has the friend console her (இனி நீ ஆற்றல் வேண்டும்). Only Manakkudavar on 1235 says இயற்பழித்து outright; Parimelazhagar's 1235 is 'how shall we hide it'. Manakkudavar takes தூற்றார் in 1190 as the townspeople, not the friend.

title: The goddess of fortune and her elder sister: one figure, many doorsteps
claim: The Kural personifies fortune as a goddess (செய்யாள் in 84, செய்யவள் in 167, திரு in 179, 482 and 920, தாமரையினாள் in 617) and misfortune as her elder sister (தவ்வை in 167, மாமுகடி in 617, முகடி in 936), and the figure recurs across both books with a different moral trigger each time. She settles in the home of the glad-faced host (84), leaves the envious man and hands him to her sister (167), seeks out those who know virtue and do not covet (179), lives in the labour of the unslothful while her sister lives in sloth (617), is tied down by timely action (482), has already abandoned those who keep two-minded women, drink and dice (920), and in 936 gambling is her sister under another name, which Parimelazhagar explains by saying the sister's real name is too ill-omened to speak. 594 gives the same personification without the goddess: ஆக்கம் asks the way to the man of unwavering energy. Taken together, the verses show the goddess is a portable image that each chapter lends to its own virtue, generosity, non-envy, non-coveting, exertion and timing, not a doctrine about what in fact draws wealth; and 371 undercuts the residence rule of 617 by making sloth and effort themselves products of fate.
limits: The thread claims a shared figure, not a theology: Kalaignar reads the two goddesses of 617 as mere names for the industrious and the idle. The verses never rank the triggers against each other, and the fate question raised by 371 belongs to thread:fate_and_agency. The first word of 594 is truncated in this edition (க்கம் for ஆக்கம்).
audit_issue: The recurring figure is well documented, but the conclusion that it is 'a portable image ... not a doctrine about what in fact draws wealth' goes beyond the verses. Having many triggers does not make them non-causal, and Parimelazhagar treats 617 as stating the cause (ஏது) of fortune and misfortune. In 482 he glosses திரு simply as செல்வம் with no goddess, so counting it among the goddess's names is a reading.

title: Wrongly got gain: refused because it fails, and refused even if it succeeds
claim: The Kural refuses wealth got by wrong means on two different grounds that sit side by side. One set argues from outcome: gain by coveting turns out badly when enjoyed (177), stolen gain perishes while seeming to grow (283), what is taken with others' tears leaves with tears (659), wealth made by deceit is water in an unfired pot (660), and wrongdoing to escape poverty only renews it (205). The other set concedes that the gain is real and good and still rules it out, using a fixed concessive form: நன்றே தரினும் (113), நன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் பெரிதெனினும் (328), செல்வம் பெறினும் (311), அடுக்கிய கோடி பெறினும் (954), வென்றிடினும் (931), and 657 ranks the utter poverty of the worthy above blame-laden wealth. The concessive verses make the prohibition independent of the prediction, so it stands where 177 or 205 might fail. The Book of Wealth carries the rule into acquisition itself: the promise that wealth yields virtue and pleasure (754, 760) is restricted to wealth that came திறனறிந்து தீதின்றி, 755 orders wealth without grace and love to be let go with the same verb விடல் as 113, and 1009 says such wealth is taken by others.
limits: The two grounds do not contradict each other and the book never says which is primary. On Parimelazhagar, 311 concerns yogic powers and 328 sacrificial killing by renunciants, so reading them as general rules about wealth follows Pope and Kalaignar rather than his gloss. 754 and 760 are addressed to the king.
audit_issue: 931 is misfiled in the concessive set: it grants வென்றிடினும் but then argues from the outcome (வென்றதூஉம் தூண்டிற்பொன் மீன்விழுங்கி அற்று), so it does not show the prohibition holding apart from a prediction. 1009 sits in the chapter on wealth that does no good (நன்றியில்செல்வம்), and Parimelazhagar reads it as the miser's unspent hoard, not wrongly acquired wealth; only Manakkudavar and Kalaignar put its அன்பொரீஇ ... அறநோக்காது at the stage of acquisition. 954's குன்றுவ is any degrading act, not a way of getting wealth.

title: Owning is not having: wealth measured by its holder
claim: In both books the Kural denies that holding goods amounts to having them unless the holder has some further quality, and it states this in one recurring form, 'whatever they have, they have nothing': a wife without worth (53, உள்ளதென் இல்லவள் மாணாக்கடை), a person without understanding (430, என்னுடையரேனும் இலர்; 841 calls want of understanding இன்மையுள் இன்மை), one without energy (591, உடையது உடையரோ), one who neither gives nor enjoys (1005, கோடியுண்டாயினும் இல்). The same judgment is pushed further into an inversion of wealth over poverty when the holder is wrong: wealth with the unlearned hurts more than poverty with the good (408), having hurts more than not having under an unjust king (558), great wealth with the discourteous is milk spoiled by its vessel (1000), with the grim-faced it is as if seen by a ghost (565), with a fool it feeds strangers while kin starve (837). The paired images fix where the fault lies: 660 blames the making (unfired pot) and 1000 the holder (bad vessel, good milk); 216 and 1008 put the same fruiting tree in the same village and let the holder's character decide whether it feeds or poisons.
limits: This is a claim about the condition under which பொருள் counts as உடைமை, not about which thing deserves the name செல்வம் (thread:true_wealth). The chapter on making wealth pulls the other way, 751 and 752 saying wealth alone gives standing and everyone honours the rich, though 973 and 1002 qualify those in turn. Parimelazhagar grounds 430 and 591 alike in the holder's inability to keep or remake wealth, which is narrower than the verses' wording.
audit_issue: 558 does not fit 'when the holder is wrong': its condition is the unjust king (முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்), not any defect in the one who has the wealth. 53 likewise puts the deciding quality in the wife, not the holder. 216 and 1008 are a counter-image of two different trees (பயன்மரம், நச்சு மரம்), not 'the same fruiting tree'.

title: Understanding as foresight, and its limits
claim: In the Book of Wealth அறிவு is repeatedly defined as knowing and guarding against what is coming: 427 makes knowing what will be the mark of the wise, 429 promises them no shaking affliction, and 435 and 535 give the failure two outcomes, sudden ruin and late regret. The book then qualifies this in three directions: the foresight can be obtained through others the ruler keeps (442), understanding also dissolves trouble that has already come (622), and 372 says a fate of loss makes a person foolish, which Parimelazhagar extends to one who has every understanding. Read together, foresight is the working core of understanding in statecraft, but neither wholly one's own nor proof against fate.
limits: The verses do not say foresight is the whole of அறிவு; elsewhere the term is tested morally (203, 315) and by seeing the real (355). The pull between 372 and 429 belongs with the fate-and-agency conflict and is not resolved in the verses.
audit_issue: Only 427 and 429 tie the foresight to அறிவு; 435 and 535 speak of guarding before (வருமுன்னர், முன்னுற) without the word, and Parimelazhagar reads them as guarding against faults and against enemies exploiting a lapse. Parimelazhagar also records an alternative reading of 427's ஆவதறிவார் as 'know what is good for them'.

title: Does understanding follow the world or test it?
claim: Several verses make accord with the world part of what understanding is: the much-studied who cannot move with the world lack understanding (140), to live as the world lives is அறிவு (426), and even after knowing a method one should act knowing how the world goes (637). 850 extends this from conduct to belief: one who denies what the world affirms is set down as a demon. Yet 423, in the same chapter as 426, defines understanding as finding the true substance of a thing whoever says it. Parimelazhagar narrows 'the world' in 140 and 850 to the high-minded many and reads 426 as advice to a king, and Kalaignar's 'shown by evidence' moves 850 toward 423.
limits: On Parimelazhagar's reading 214 also makes knowing the way of the world the test of being alive, but Manakkudavar takes ஒத்தது there as ஒப்புரவு, so it is weak support. The 850-423 conflict is already noted under knowing_and_learning; this thread concerns the world as a standard, not the speaker's standing.
audit_issue: The narrowing of 'world' to the high-minded is not Parimelazhagar's alone: Kalaignar also glosses 140 and 426 by உயர்ந்தோர். Parimelazhagar on 637 grounds the rule in avoiding blame (செய்யின் அது பழிக்கும்), which is prudential rather than epistemic.

title: The sulk: love's best part, in measure
claim: The Book of Love keeps returning to ஊடல், and its verses raise and then bound it. 1109 lists sulking with reconciliation and union as love's rewards; 1326 ranks sulking above union, as digestion above eating; 1330, the book's last verse, calls it love's pleasure but places its own pleasure in the embrace that follows. 1302 and 1306 make it a matter of degree, salt that seasons and spoils if prolonged, fruit unripe or overripe without it, and 1282 says that when love is full not a millet-seed of sulking is wanted. Together they treat the sulk as valuable only as a measured step toward union, which Parimelazhagar makes explicit in glossing 1109 and 1330 as ending it at the right point.
limits: The verses come from different speakers and situations (1282 is the woman's impatience voiced as general advice, per Parimelazhagar), so this is a pattern across voices, not one doctrine. Pope's translation of 1109 as lust is a translator's reading.
audit_issue: '1330, the book's last verse' holds only in Parimelazhagar's order; Manakkudavar closes the Book of Love at 1323. The commentators assign கனி and கருக்காய் in 1306 to துனி and புலவி differently: Parimelazhagar takes கனி as rich ripeness, not spoilage.

title: Love measured against liquor
claim: The Book of Love uses liquor, which chapter 93 condemns, as its standard comparison for love, and uses it both ways. In 1090, 1201 and 1281 love surpasses toddy: liquor delights only when drunk, love at a look or a thought, from first sight (1090) through separation (1201) to the woman's longing (1281). In 1145 and 1288 love instead works like drink: wanted more with each exposure, and in 1288 craved though it does shameful harm, which Parimelazhagar spells out as loss of shame, restraint, conduct and awareness, the very charges laid against drink in chapter 93.
limits: The chapter 93 verses are not in this packet; the link to them rests on Parimelazhagar's gloss of 1288. Speakers differ by commentator for 1090, 1145 and 1288, so the thread does not claim a single voice holds both views.
audit_issue: In 1145 the thing that grows sweeter is love's becoming rumour (Parimelazhagar: காமம் அலராந்தோறும் இனிது), not love at each meeting, so 'wanted more with each exposure' means public exposure.

title: How does a harmful deed return to the doer?
claim: Across the chapters on fearing evil deeds, not harming, not coveting, not stealing and clean action, the return of harm is described in several distinct ways rather than one. Its inescapability is spatial in 207 and 208 (the enmity of deeds follows and kills, ruin stays at the foot like a shadow, both with வீயாது), and 313 sharpens it with உய்யா: an enemy can be survived, one's own hurtful act cannot. It is temporal in 319 (forenoon harm comes back in the afternoon, தாமே, of itself), an agent's act in 204 (அறம் plots the plotter's ruin), and a near-tautology of desire in 206 and 320 (whoever wants no pain causes none). A separate figure, the ripening, places the harm at the harvest and not at the getting: coveted gain in 177, theft in 284, and forbidden deeds that succeed in 658 all go bad at விளைவு, and 659 extends the return to wealth taken with tears, while adding that rightly got wealth pays later even if lost.
limits: The thread describes how the return is pictured, not whether the book thinks it always happens; 169 concedes that the crooked prosper and the upright fall, which thread:justice_of_the_world takes up. Who or what returns the harm (அறம் in 204, nobody in 319, Parimelazhagar's அறக்கடவுள் and pāvam in his glosses) is left unsettled by the verses.
audit_issue: 658 does not use விளைவு; its timing comes only from முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும் (even when the deed succeeds), so it belongs to the ripening figure by sense rather than by wording. 284's harvest is of love of stealing (களவின்கண் கன்றிய காதல்), not of stolen gain as such.

title: One checklist for action, from the king's deed to the minister's definition
claim: A short list of conditions for successful action recurs across five Porul chapters and changes role as it moves. In 483 means and time (கருவி, காலம்) make any 'hard deed' (அருவினை) possible; 631 reuses the same three words but turns them into the definition of a minister, adding method (செய்கை); 675 expands them into a five-item rule for anyone acting (resources, means, time, deed, place); and 516, in the chapter on employing people, keeps deed and time and adds the one item the others lack, the doer. A parallel pair, 461 and 676, shares the closing command (சூழ்ந்து / பார்த்துச் செயல்) and the yield as its last term, but 461 counts loss against gain while 676 weighs the course of the work, its completion and obstacles. Read together, the minister's defining skill is the general checklist for action, and the book adjusts the list to the chapter it sits in.
limits: This is a claim about recurring vocabulary and list structure, not that the lists are meant as one doctrine; Parimelazhagar glosses the items differently in each place (in 675 each term covers both one's own side and the enemy's). It does not cover the separate theme of execution failing after sound planning (640, 664).
audit_issue: The 461 and 676 pair shares none of the கருவி/காலம் vocabulary, so it is a second, parallel list rather than part of the same checklist, and its closing verbs differ (சூழ்ந்து, பார்த்து). Parimelazhagar reads 483's actor as the king (அரசரால்).

title: Can a single virtue stand without the rest?
claim: Several verses isolate one restraint and say it keeps its value even when the rest of virtue is absent, using a shared 'even if he does wrong' frame: not desiring another's wife in 150 (அறன்வரையான் அல்ல செயினும்) and not backbiting in 181 (அறங்கூறான் அல்ல செயினும்), with 142 ranking the adulterer lowest among those outside virtue. 297 goes further for not lying, saying the other virtues may be left undone, and 296 gives the reason: not lying yields all the virtues by itself. Yet 321 answers 'what is virtuous action?' with not killing, and 33 tells one to do virtue everywhere and without break. Because the book makes this move for different virtues, the verses read best as emphasis on each chapter's virtue, and Parimelazhagar on 150 and 181 says only that the one quality 'stands out' despite the faults, not that it suffices.
limits: Only 296-297 claim sufficiency; 150 and 181 claim only that the one abstention is still good. Parimelazhagar reconciles 297 with 33 by reading it as advice to keep one virtue unfailingly rather than fail at many, and 323 itself ranks not killing above not lying (see thread:competing_supremes and thread:truth_by_effect).
audit_issue: Parimelazhagar narrows 142's அறன்கடை நின்றார் to those in sin through desire, so it ranks adulterers among lovers gone wrong rather than among all who stand outside virtue. Kalaignar reads 150 as a comparison (desiring another's wife is worse than straying from virtue), not as the 'even if' frame.

title: Does virtue yield wealth, or wealth yield virtue?
claim: Book 1 says virtue yields distinction and wealth (31, சிறப்பு ஈனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும்), and Book 2 turns the same construction round: wealth that came by knowing the means and without wrong yields virtue and pleasure (754, அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்), and for those who amass bright wealth the other two come easily together (760). The reversal holds only with a condition on how the wealth was got: 754's தீதின்றி fits wealth into 39's rule that only pleasure through virtue is pleasure, 659 says what is taken with tears leaves with tears, and 1009 uses 760's own word ஒண்பொருள் for wealth amassed by ignoring virtue, which others carry off. So the two books do not rank the ends differently; they make the causal arrow run both ways and let the manner of acquisition decide which way it runs.
limits: The condition is explicit in 754 but only read into 760 by Parimelazhagar, who glosses ஒண்பொருள் there as wealth that comes by the right way; on its face 760 promises virtue to abundance as such. Parimelazhagar also reads 754 as a king's revenue raised without tyranny, so its scope may be royal wealth only.
audit_issue: Parimelazhagar reads 31's சிறப்பு as liberation and its செல்வம் as heaven and similar rewards (துறக்கம் முதலிய செல்வம்), so on his reading 31 is not about worldly wealth and the 'reversal' with 754 is only verbal. 1009's fault is not how the wealth was got but its hoarding: Parimelazhagar glosses அறநோக்காது as not giving to the poor and அன்பொரீஇ as dropping love so as not to give. 1009 therefore shows use, not manner of acquisition, deciding the outcome, and its own ஒண்பொருள் cuts against reading 760's ஒண்பொருள் as 'rightly got'.

title: Is the lovers' sulk a pleasure, and on what terms?
claim: The Book of Love praises the sulk in rising terms: one of love's rewards (1109), sweeter than union (1326), beyond heaven (1323), love's very pleasure (1330). Almost every praise is hedged by a condition stated nearby. It must be measured like salt and spoils if prolonged (1302), only a small துனி is wanted (1322), yet love without any quarrel is fruit at the wrong stage (1306). It is sweet only if the embrace follows (1330, கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்), the doubt about that sequel is its own pain (1307), and it is sweet only with one who loves (1309). 1326 puts the sulk above union, and 1330 makes its sweetness depend on union.
limits: These are speeches by characters, not a treatise; 1282, which says no sulk at all is wanted when love is full, is on Parimelazhagar's reading the woman's impatience dressed as advice. The conditions limit the praise but are never offered as a retraction of it.
audit_issue: 1322 does not say that 'only a small துனி is wanted'. It says the small துனி that a sulk brings leads to greatness even if his grace droops; 'only' comes from pairing it with Parimelazhagar's துனி/புலவி distinction on 1306. Manakkudavar reads 1322 as the sulk being pleasant even without union, which cuts against the claim that union is the condition.

title: A sulk that needs no offence
claim: In chapter 132 the man lists sulks with thinner and thinner grounds: a wreath (1313), his attempt to appease her (1319), a silent look (1320), each drawing anger (காயும்). Only 1311 states a ground, other women's eyes on him. Chapter 133 then has both speakers concede there is no fault: she says he has none, yet his tenderness can bring on a sulk (1321, இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு), and he says that though men are faultless, being kept from her arms has its own savour (1325, தவறிலர் ஆயினும்); on Parimelazhagar's reading 1305 says the same. Read together, the book detaches the sulk from wrongdoing and treats the groundless sulk of chapter 132 as a pleasure in chapter 133.
limits: Manakkudavar reads 1305's நல்லவர் as the other women, and Parimelazhagar explains 1321 by her thought that others too may receive his tenderness, so jealousy survives with its ground removed. Real offence is not absent from these chapters: 1311 names him பரத்த.
audit_issue: 'Only 1311 states a ground' undersells chapter 132: in 1313, 1319 and 1320 she also names a ground, always another woman (ஒருத்தியைக் காட்டிய, பிறர்க்கும், யாருள்ளி). The difference is that the man calls those grounds baseless, not that she gives none.

title: Can one live through separation, and why does she?
claim: Several speeches say separation cannot be survived: parting is death to his life (1124), news of his quick return is for those still alive then (1151), and on Parimelazhagar's reading 1160's 'many endure the parting and live on' is irony. 1198 turns survival into a charge: none are harder (வன்கண்) than those who live on without a kind word, the word 1156 had applied to him for announcing the parting. Yet the same speaker is later alive and gives reasons: she lives by seeing him in dreams (1213) and by longing for his return (1263), the very return 1151 dismissed. Taken together, the verses deny that she can survive, then accuse her of surviving, then name what keeps her alive.
limits: This is a dramatic sequence, not a teaching about grief. Speakers vary by commentator (Manakkudavar gives 1151 to the woman), and Parimelazhagar takes 1213 as said to reassure the friend, so its explanation may be partly for show.
audit_issue: 1124 is a simile (சாதல் அதற்கன்னள்) spoken by the man at a brief daytime parting on Parimelazhagar's reading, so it says separation feels like death more than that it cannot be survived. On Parimelazhagar, 1198 is the woman's self-reproach (யான் வன்கண்ணேனாகலின்), which is what lets it count as the charge against her.

title: The body testifies; who decides what it proves?
claim: In the separation chapters her body speaks before she does: slipping bangles broadcast his leaving (1157, தூற்றா), shoulders announce it (1233), the bangles knew it before she did (1277), and she has been pale seven days though he left yesterday (1278; also 1185). All parties accept this evidence, but they dispute its verdict. The town reads the pallor as news about her and never says he left her (1188); the friend reads the wasted shoulders as declaring the cruel one's cruelty (1235); and she refuses that inference, pained to hear him called cruel (1236).
limits: Speaker assignments differ (Parimelazhagar gives 1233 and 1235 to the friend, Manakkudavar to the woman), and Parimelazhagar's 'before' in 1277 depends on reading the parting as one of mind while they are still together. She herself uses கொடியார் கொடுமை of him in 1169, so her refusal in 1236 is of the charge from another's mouth.
audit_issue: Parimelazhagar takes 1157's bangles as telling the friend (உனக்கு அறிவியாவோ), not broadcasting to the town, and he reads 1185 as recalling an earlier departure, so the public and immediate force the claim gives these two rests on the plain wording.

title: What can friendship survive?
claim: The book says those devoted to friendship do not leave a friend once made (791, நட்டபின் வீடில்லை) and that the world loves those who do not give up old friends (809), yet it calls leaving a fool's friendship gain (797) and orders the unfit dropped even at a price (800, ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக). It also says the bond grows with practice (783) yet does not need it (785), and on Manakkudavar's reading 785's quick bond sits against 792's demand to examine again and again. The growth question is settled by character, not time: the bond with பண்புடையார் deepens with practice (783), while with பண்பிலார் shrinking is better than growing (811), the waning that 782 observes in fools' friendship. Parimelazhagar supplies the limit on leaving: exit is for a friendship taken up without knowing (800).
limits: On Parimelazhagar's reading 785 only says feeling, more than contact, makes the bond, and there is no conflict with 783 or 792. Old friends who harm you are kept (807), which he treats as a separate case.
audit_issue: The claim says the growth question is 'settled by character, not time', but 783 against 785 is about whether contact is needed to make the bond (புணர்ச்சி பழகுதல் வேண்டா), which 811's பண்பிலார் does not address; character settles only whether growth is desirable. 783 itself speaks of growing delight (நயம்), not of a bond that needs practice.

title: The friend is judged at the hour of ruin
claim: In all three books one moment decides a friendship: what the friend does when the other falls. The Book of Virtue says never abandon those who were a support in sorrow (106) and that their help is remembered through seven births (107); chapter 79 defines friendship as sharing the suffering in ruin (787) and acting there and then like a hand catching a slipping garment (788). The same measure condemns: the deserter's bond burns the heart even at death (799), those who fail at the crisis are an untrained horse worse than solitude (814, 798's ஆற்றறுப்பார்), and friends who give no safety are better never acquired (815). In the Book of Love, 1293 turns the saying that the ruined have no friends against the speaker's own heart, a deserter she cannot decline.
limits: This is one standard among several: other verses make rebuke (784, 795) or inner feeling (785, 786) the mark of friendship. 1293 is a lover's dramatised reproach quoting a saying, not a teaching about friends.

title: Learning that conduct cancels
claim: 391 asks for two things in order: learn without flaw, then stand in keeping with it. Several verses across the Books of Virtue and Wealth enforce the second half by withdrawing the status of the learned from those who skip it: whoever has learned much but cannot move in accord with the world is unlearned and without understanding (140); whoever has read, understood and taught but is not restrained is the greatest fool (834); wide understanding is worth nothing if one covets (175); and restraint after learning is what virtue itself seeks out (130). In statecraft and medicine the same rule becomes professional: knowing the method from the treatises, act knowing the world (637), and the learned physician must weigh this patient, this illness, this time (949).
limits: The verses do not claim that study produces good conduct; 823 says study rarely makes the unworthy good at heart, which is why 391 has to command conduct separately. The thread does not cover the question of where understanding comes from, treated in thread:knowing_and_learning.
audit_issue: 637 and 949 are about fitting treatise knowledge to circumstances, not about conduct cancelling learning, so 'the same rule becomes professional' stretches the thread's rule. Parimelazhagar reads மாணார் in 823 as enemies who do not turn friend through study, not as the unworthy in general, so the limits lean on a broader reading than the chapter gives.

title: Learning that is not spoken
claim: The book ranks learned people by whether they can deliver their learning before an audience, and is harsh to those who cannot. Those who cannot unfold what they learned are scentless flowers (650); those who cannot speak tellingly in a good assembly are useless however much they learned (728); and those who learned yet fear the assembly are lower than the unlearned (729), using the very word கடை that 395 gives the unlearned. Silence is therefore graded by who keeps it: it is the unlearned person's merit before the learned (403) and the learned person's disgrace. The positive title follows the same measure: 'learned among the learned' is whoever makes learning go home before the learned (722), and the envoy is judged the same way among treatise-holders and in a hostile court (683, 686, 724).
limits: These verses concern speech before assemblies and courts, mostly in the Book of Wealth's chapters on speech and assemblies; they do not say learning has no private worth (398 makes it a protection across births). 720 adds that an unfit audience wastes even good speech.
audit_issue: 683 concerns the envoy's mastery of statecraft treatises among ministers (நூலாருள் நூல்வல்லன்), not delivering speech, so it adds little to the claim about voicing. Parimelazhagar puts the failure in 728 and 729 down to fear (அச்சத்தான்), which separates the chapter on the assembly from 650's plain inability to expound.

title: Where is wealth kept safe?
claim: Across the Book of Virtue and the Book of Wealth, a run of verses turns the hoarder's own logic of keeping against him. Feeding the destitute is the place to deposit wealth (226, வைப்புழி; Parimelazhagar: what is so given comes back to help the giver), while those who keep what they own lose it (228, வைத்திழக்கும்), eating alone to fill one's store is worse than begging (229), the man who does not even use his heap is as dead (1001), and wealth withheld from the destitute ages unused like a beauty growing old alone (1007). The positive side recurs in three chapters: shared food keeps hunger from the sharer (227), keeps his line from failing (44), and gain belongs only to those who, like the crow, call others before eating (527).
limits: The book does not rest giving on return alone: 228 names giving's own joy and 222 calls giving good even if there were no higher world. 82 and 229 condemn the solitary meal by comparison rather than by consequence, and the protective results in 44, 227 and 527 are asserted, not argued.
audit_issue: Only 226 and 228 turn the hoarder's logic of keeping (வை-) against him in their own words; 1001 and 1007 condemn wealth left unused rather than wealth lost by being kept. 82, cited only in the limits, concerns hospitality to a guest and does not bear on storing wealth.

title: Giving and the manner that goes with it
claim: The book rarely praises giving bare: it pairs it with a glad face, sweet words, no scorn or no anger, and once ranks the manner above the gift, since 92 says a glad face and sweet speech are better than giving with a glad heart. 953 lists smile, giving, sweet words and not scorning flatly as marks of a good lineage (Parimelazhagar: the way one meets the poor who come), and 1057 shows why scorn matters, since the asker rejoices at giving without contempt, while 224 has the giver's own unease end only at the asker's glad face. In the Book of Wealth the same pair becomes an instrument: giving with sweet words wins the world for a king (387) and surrounds a man with kin (525), and 526 swaps sweet speech for not cherishing anger; Parimelazhagar on 525 matches the pair to the northern texts' dana and sama.
limits: 92 sits in the chapter praising sweet speech and may be that chapter's emphasis rather than a fixed ranking. Other verses define real giving by its recipient, not its manner (221, 223), and 387 and 525 treat giving as a means to loyalty, which is not the same claim as 92's ethical ranking.
audit_issue: 'The book rarely praises giving bare' is overstated: most of chapter 23 (ஈகை) and 231 to 232 praise giving with no word on manner, which is more than the limits' recipient verses 221 and 223. 224 is about the giver's discomfort ending when the asker is satisfied, not about the manner of giving.

title: One word for two shames
claim: 1011 splits நாண் in two: real shame is shame at one's deeds, and the rest is the shame of women of fair brow (Parimelazhagar: restraint of mind, speech and body proper to women of family). The Book of Love's shame is the second kind: in 1163 and 1247 it is, on Parimelazhagar's reading, what stops the woman telling him or going to him, and in 1251 it is the bolt on the door of restraint. Yet the Book of Love prizes that shame in the first kind's terms: it is the ornament that makes jewels needless (1089, as moral shame is the ornament of the worthy in 1014), and it is held dearer than life (Parimelazhagar on 1297; 1163's life strained on the pole), which is the valuation 1017 gives moral shame.
limits: The love verses are dramatised speeches, and the bridge to 1014 and 1017 is partly the commentator's: 1297 itself does not say shame is dearer than life. Kalaignar reads 1014 as remorse for a fault and Pope translates நாண் in 1017 as modesty, so the line between the two shames is drawn differently by different readers.
audit_issue: 1163 does not rank shame above life: on Parimelazhagar love and shame hang in equal balance (ஒன்றினொன்று மிகாது) on the life-pole, so it supports 1017's valuation only loosely.

title: In the Book of Love shame never holds
claim: Several lover-speakers set shame against desire, and in none of them does shame survive; what varies is how it goes. 1247 puts the choice to the heart (give up desire or shame, I cannot bear both); 1132 makes it by decision, setting shame aside to ride the palmyra horse; in 1134 the flood of love carries shame off and in 1251 the axe of desire breaks the door it bolted; in 1297 it is forgotten in his absence, and in 1257 it is simply not felt in his presence (Parimelazhagar: on his return from another woman). Read together, the dilemma 1247 states is settled by force, forgetting or reunion as often as by choice.
limits: These are separate dramatised moments, and reading them as one sequence follows the chapter order, not any statement in the text. 1163 holds love and shame in balance without a loss, and 1149 is about shame at gossip rather than at desire. The man also loses shame by force in 1134, which qualifies the existing gender_asymmetry contrast between his choosing and her bearing.
audit_issue: The title 'never holds' overreaches the Book of Love: 1137 praises the woman who suffers a sea of desire and still does not mount the மடல் (கடலன்ன காமம் உழந்தும் மடலேறாப் பெண்), so her restraint holds there. The claim is accurate only for the verses it cites. The 1297-1247 note's 'the chapter between them' is wrong, since 1247 is in chapter 125 and 1297 in chapter 130.

title: The inside decides what counts
claim: Several verses in different domains apply one test: an outward act counts only if the mind behind it matches. Virtue is wholly a spotless mind and the rest is noisy show (34), and firmness in action is wholly firmness of mind with all else 'பிற' (661), in the same shape. Sweet speech is virtue because it comes from within (93), friendship is the smile of the heart, not the face (786), straight speech is rectitude only if there is no bend within (119), and truth spoken with the mind outranks austerity and giving (295, 294). Ritual bathing is the case in point: water reaches only the outside (298), and many bathe with impure minds (278).
limits: The book does not make the mind self-sufficient: 455 and 459 say purity and goodness of mind rest on purity of company. It also asks elsewhere whether the inside can be read from outside at all (thread:signs_and_faces), and 829 permits a show of friendship toward enemies (thread:ethics_vs_statecraft).
audit_issue: 661 is about firmness, not about outward acts being genuine; it shares only the shape of 34. 298 does not say water reaches 'only' the outside; it pairs outer purity from water with inner purity seen through truth.

title: One promise, several conditions: you obtain what you think of
