claim: The book makes nearly the same promise, that one obtains what one has thought of (உள்ளியது / எண்ணிய ... எய்தும்), three times and attaches a different inner condition each time: never harbouring anger (309), keeping one's mind on the goal without forgetting (540), and firmness (666). Parimelazhagar assigns these to different people, 309 to the ascetic and 540 to the king, so one formula serves both Aram and Porul. The power of thought reaches suffering too: a flood of trouble perishes when the wise person merely thinks it through (622), yet 7 says the mind's anxiety is hard to remove except for those who reach the feet of the incomparable one.
limits: The three conditions are not rivals; commentators treat each as sufficient within its own chapter's concern. The 7-622 conflict holds only on Manakkudavar's wider reading of மனக்கவலை; Parimelazhagar narrows 7 to the sorrows of rebirth, which 622 does not address.

title: Is the beloved the cure for love's sickness?
claim: Several verses make the one who causes the sickness its only medicine: one look in her eyes wounds and the other heals (1091), she is herself the medicine for the disease she gives (1102), and the woman says one day of his return would destroy all her sickness (1266). This explains why her heart can name no medicine at all in 1241, and 1275 finds the remedy only in a sign. Yet other verses deny that presence cures: union itself now holds the pain of fearing separation (1152), her eyes do not sleep whether he comes or not (1179), and her heart fears not having him and, having him, fears parting (1295).
limits: The cure verses 1091 and 1102 belong to the man in the first meetings, while the denials are the woman's in a settled relationship facing separation, so the difference may track the stage of love rather than a contradiction. The speaker of 1275 is the man for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.
audit_issue: 1241 only asks the heart for a medicine (நினைத்தொன்று சொல்லாயோ); it does not say the heart can name none, and the claim's 'this explains why' reads 1102 into it. 1275 does not place the cure only in a sign of the beloved: on Parimelazhagar the medicine is the friend's assurance that the beloved will not part, and on Manakkudavar the friend is telling the man his suit will succeed.

title: The woman turns on her own eyes and heart
claim: Where the man finds the source of love's sickness in her eyes (1091), the woman in separation finds it in her own: her eyes showed him to her (1171), and she mocks them as laughable (1173), rejoices that they now suffer the sickness they gave (1176), and curses them to weep until their water is gone, which 1174 reports has happened (1177). Her heart is treated the same way across later chapters: thinking of him alone, her heart is there only to eat her (1296), remembering burns it (1207), and she rebukes it for sitting and suffering over one who has no pity (1243).
limits: Chapters 118, 125 and 130 are built around addressing the eyes or the heart, so the pattern partly follows the book's chapter scheme; the claim is that the same self-division runs across them, not that it is a hidden theme. On Parimelazhagar's reading of 1296 the heart's harm comes from dwelling on his cruelties, not from memory as such.
audit_issue: 1207 does not turn on the heart: in உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும் the heart is what is burned, the victim of memory and separation, so it fits the self-division theme less than 1243 and 1296, where the heart is blamed.

title: Does remembering the absent lover comfort or wound?
claim: Chapter 121 opens by calling remembrance an unfailing joy: love is sweeter than toddy because even thinking of it gives delight that does not end (1201), and thinking of the beloved brings no pain (1202); the woman makes the same toddy comparison in 1281. The same chapter and later ones then make thinking the source of pain: even remembering burns (1207), her life wastes as she dwells on his want of grace (1209), and when she sits alone and thinks, her heart eats her (1296). Parimelazhagar separates the cases by what is remembered: past union in 1201, his neglect in 1209, his cruelties in 1296. Yet forgetting is refused as worse (1207, 1262), while 1250 argues that keeping him in her heart costs her beauty, the very loss 1262 attributes to forgetting.
limits: These are dramatised speeches in different moods, not a doctrine of memory, and the speaker assignments (man in 1201 and 1202) are Parimelazhagar's; Manakkudavar gives 1202 to the woman and reads it as conditional. The gender side of 1202/1207 is already in thread:gender_asymmetry.
audit_issue: On Parimelazhagar, what the woman remembers in 1207 is the past union (அவ்வின்பத்தை), the same object as 1201, and it is the separation that burns, so 'what is remembered' does not separate every case. He also reads 1250's கவின் as the inner beauty left after the outer is lost, so it is not quite 'the very loss' of 1262's காரிகை and bangles.

title: He lives in her heart: a defence that becomes a doubt
claim: In chapters 113 and 122 the woman answers the charge that her lover is absent and loveless by locating him inside herself: in her eyes (1126), in her heart gladly and always while the town says he lives apart (1129, 1130), on her shoulder in sleep and in her heart on waking (1218), so that her heart has no one to go looking for (1249). Parimelazhagar frames several of these as replies to the friend's blame of him. In chapter 121 the same image turns: he is always in her heart, but is she in his (1204)? He bars her from his heart and is not ashamed to keep entering hers (1205), and by 1243 his lack of any pitying thought is a settled premise. Her body also contradicts the claim of presence in 1184, where constant thought does not stop the pallor.
limits: The sequence is the reader's arrangement across chapters, not a stated argument; 1205's guarded heart is read as accusation by Manakkudavar. The thread does not claim the man's verses share this doubt.
audit_issue: 1249 is in chapter 125, not 113 or 122. Parimelazhagar ties 1184 to her recalling his parting promises (தெளிவித்த சொற்கள்) and treats the pallor as the body betraying mind and speech; reading it as undercutting 'presence in her heart' is the writer's framing.

title: Is good family the source of conduct or its name?
claim: 133 defines good family as conduct (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை) and says a lapse becomes low birth, and 1019 agrees that a lapse in principle burns one's lineage. Chapter 96 runs the other way: integrity and shame are natural only to the well-born (951), the well-born do not slip in conduct, truth and shame (952), and a lapse only makes people doubt a man's lineage (958), keeping birth as the underlying fact. The selection verses rely on chapter 96's direction, asking for good family alongside shame when choosing an officer (502) or a friend (794); on 133's definition that first test cannot be checked apart from the second.
limits: The conflict depends on reading 133 as dissolving birth into conduct; Parimelazhagar reads it within varna, as conduct keeping or losing a rank birth already gave, which removes it. This complements thread:birth_across_book (972 and the screening verses) rather than replacing it, since its 972 links are not in this packet.
audit_issue: Kalaignar reads 951, 952 and 502 in 133's direction (those who keep these are to be counted well-born), so chapter 96's 'birth first' direction is Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's construal more than the bare Tamil. 958's failing is specifically நாரின்மை, lack of kindness (Parimelazhagar: not giving, harsh speech), not any lapse in conduct.

title: The family as something built, not inherited
claim: Where chapter 96 treats குடி as inherited character, chapters 61 and 103 treat it as something kept up or raised by work: those who want their family to be a family must drive out sloth (602), the family lengthens through long effort and mature knowledge (1022), and for the slothful it dies down while faults multiply (604). The same double penalty on the family and in fault is attached to covetousness in 171, and 609 makes the decline reversible once a man ends sloth's rule over him. 1028 turns this against honour: the family-builder who idles and stands on dignity (மானம்) ruins the family, whereas 961, as Parimelazhagar glosses it, gives up even indispensable things that would lower one's birth.
limits: The two views are not set against each other by the text; one chapter says what a family is, the other what its members owe it, and 1022/1028 can be read as about a clan's prosperity rather than its rank. The 961/1028 tension depends on reading both as concerning the family's standing.
audit_issue: The opening contrast with chapter 96, where குடி is inherited, has no link of its own and is asserted rather than shown. Kalaignar reads 1028's மானம் as being shaken by insults rather than standing on dignity, which would weaken the 961 tension.

title: Can greatness survive one small lapse?
claim: Several verses in different books grant a person great stature and then make it hang on a single act. 124 sets the restrained householder's stature above a mountain, and 974 says greatness exists only while one keeps hold of oneself; 965 states the loss as a rule, that even the hill-like sink (குன்றுவர்) for a lowering act the size of a kunri seed, while 144 (entering another's home) and 195 (idle speech) name particular acts that undo a person's worth however great. 898 uses the same hill pun for the opposite direction: the hill-like can bring others to nothing, so in the book's imagery height gives power over others but no protection against one's own lapse.
limits: The verses do not say greatness can never be regained; they only make its loss quick and cheap. Parimelazhagar reads the hill-like of 965 as those great by birth and those of 898 as ascetics, so the 'height' is not one kind of standing throughout.
audit_issue: On Manakkudavar, 898's குன்ற மதிப்பின் means others slighting the hill-like (அவமதித்தல்), so the hill-like are the ones diminished there too and the 'opposite direction' contrast holds only on Parimelazhagar's reading of them as ascetics who wish ruin.

title: Greatness measured by hard deeds, from renouncer to householder
claim: 26, in the chapter on renouncers, defines the great as those who do what is hard to do and the small as those who cannot; 975, in the Book of Wealth, says the same of those who have greatness, with no renunciation in view (Parimelazhagar adds: even when they are poor). 611 turns the definition into a process, saying effort itself produces the greatness a hard task needs, and 1021 puts the highest dignity in the resolve not to stop work. 505 and 972 generalise the test: deeds are the touchstone of greatness and smallness, and distinction differs by the work done though birth is alike.
limits: Parimelazhagar narrows 26's 'hard things' to yogic disciplines and reads 26 as a ranking among those of equal birth, and he takes 965's hill-like as great by birth; the book elsewhere treats birth as a real factor (see thread:birth_across_book). 26 can also be read as a fixed difference between people, which 611 does not say.
audit_issue: Parimelazhagar's gloss on 505 counts birth, quality and knowledge (பிறப்பு குணம் அறிவு) as sources of greatness and makes deeds only the test of them, so 505 does not by itself say birth is irrelevant.

title: Effort that pays whatever fate does
claim: Against 380, where fate outruns every plan, several verses give effort a return in each case fate can take. If fate denies the outcome, effort still pays the wage of the body's strain (619), and a high aim thrust aside keeps the quality of not having been thrust aside (596, which Parimelazhagar reads as thwarted by fate); if the divine helps, it girds itself and goes ahead of the one resolved to raise his family (1023), and for those who toil without delay the end comes of itself (1024). Persistence is said to trouble trouble itself (624) and to see even fate's back (620). Parimelazhagar draws the conclusion at 619: since effort is not wasted either way, one should strive without waiting on fate.
limits: This thread is about how the book secures effort's value, not whether effort is free; 371 makes effort itself a product of fate, a conflict taken up in thread:fate_and_agency. Parimelazhagar narrows 620 to fate blocking only one or two attempts.

title: Effort praised without condition, then bounded
claim: 616 says flatly that effort makes fortune and its absence brings want, and 596 sets no ceiling on aspiration, but verses elsewhere fix effort's conditions. 468 says exertion not made by the right method collapses however many guard it; 476 says that pushing beyond the tip of the branch ends one's life; 14 makes the plough, which 1031 says the whole world follows, itself depend on the rain. 739 even defines the true land as one whose wealth comes without seeking, though 1040 has the land mock those who sit idle claiming poverty.
limits: None of these verses denies that effort is necessary; they add method, measure of strength and natural supply as further conditions. The fate-based limit (371) is treated separately in thread:fate_and_agency.
audit_issue: Parimelazhagar reads 596 as addressed to kings and takes its தள்ளினும் as thwarting by fate (பால்வகை), so 596 itself concedes a limit. 739 concerns a country's natural endowment for its people, not the sufficiency of individual effort, so its pairing with 1040 is loose.

title: Which is sweeter, union or the sulk?
claim: The first union chapter sets sleeping on the beloved's soft arms above the lotus-eyed god's world (1103) and lists sulking, making up and uniting as love's rewards without ranking them (1109). The closing chapter re-ranks: sulking with one joined as water to earth outdoes heaven (1323), being kept from those same soft arms (தாம்வீழ்வார் மென்றோள், the phrase of 1103) 'has a certain something' (1325), and sulking is sweeter than union as digesting is sweeter than eating (1326). Yet the last verse makes the sulk's pleasure depend on the embrace that follows (கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின், 1330), and 1307 finds pain inside the sulk in the fear that union will be delayed, so the sulk outranks union only as a way back to it. Parimelazhagar already reads 1109's ஊடல் as needed so that union becomes sweet.
limits: These are lovers' speeches, mostly the man's in the joy-after-sulking chapter, not the author ranking pleasures in his own voice; and the ranking is of moments within one marriage, not of union against sulking as rival goods.
audit_issue: 'The last verse' (1330) is Parimelazhagar's order; Manakkudavar ends the book at 1323. Manakkudavar takes the world in 1103 as Indra's heaven, while Parimelazhagar takes it as the world ascetics attain.

title: How small a gap counts as separation?
claim: 1108 calls sweet the embrace that not even a breeze can split (வளியிடை போழப் படாஅ). Later verses test that ideal and find the threshold of separation at exactly that size: a cool breeze splitting the embrace, with the same verb போழ, pales her eyes (1239); his loosening his arms pales her forehead (1238); she shifted slightly and pallor came thick enough to scoop up (1187); pallor watches for any lapse in the embrace as darkness watches for a lamp to fail (1186). The woman and the man report it from either side. On Parimelazhagar's reading the man recalls 1238 and 1239 on his way home from a campaign, so the tiny gap is the measure against which the present separation by hills and forests is felt.
limits: 1108 itself says nothing of pallor, and Parimelazhagar frames it as a plea for marriage (union without interruption); the pallor verses are hyperbole from the separation chapters, not a separate doctrine.
audit_issue: Parimelazhagar reads 1238 and 1239 as one remembered incident (the breeze entered because he loosened his arms), so they are one threshold seen twice, not two. He reads 1186-1187 and 1238-1239 alike as a fortiori arguments: if this for a slight gap, what now in separation? That reading strengthens the claim.

title: Eyes that say what the mouth withholds
claim: Across the Book of Love, man, woman and friend all treat the eyes as a channel that speaks where the mouth does not, and that cannot be kept quiet. When eyes agree, words are useless (1100); telling love's sickness with the eyes and pleading adds womanhood to womanhood (1280, which Parimelazhagar glosses as not saying it by mouth even to her friends); eyes like beaten drums let the town learn her secret (1180); though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes go beyond her control and have something to say (1271); her pale, weeping eyes seem to tell others of his unkindness (1232). In love, concealment fails at the eyes.
limits: This holds for lovers' eyes; the Book of Wealth says enemies' smiles can hide hostility even from the face (824, see thread:signs_and_faces), so it is not a general claim that faces are honest. 1232 says only that the eyes seem to tell, and the speakers of 1100 and 1280 differ between Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar.
audit_issue: 1100 and 1280 are about eyes chosen as the channel, not eyes that betray; the claim's 'cannot be kept quiet' rests on 1180, 1271 and 1232 alone.

title: What many eyes see is no longer one's own
claim: The man disqualifies flowers as likenesses of her eyes because many people see them (பலர்காணும் பூ, 1112), and tells the moon it may resemble her face only if it stops appearing for many to see (பலர்காணத் தோன்றல், 1119); Parimelazhagar glosses both as his having her beauty for himself alone. The woman applies the same standard to him: she refuses his chest because all women feast on him in common with their eyes (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர், 1311), which Parimelazhagar takes as making it others' leftovers, and she suspects even his gaze at her of being on another woman (1320). Looking is treated as a kind of possession, by both lovers.
limits: 1311 and 1320 come from the chapter on subtle sulking, where Parimelazhagar presents the woman's charges as pretexts for a lover's sulk, and 1112 and 1119 are praise hyperbole; neither side states a rule about fidelity.
audit_issue: Only two links carry the 'seen by many' standard; 1320 is about whom he is thinking of as he looks (யாருள்ளி நோக்கினீர்), not about being seen by many, so its fit with 'looking as possession' is loose.

title: One birth's leverage on seven
claim: Several verses across Aram and Porul share a fixed arithmetic: what is done in one birth (ஒருமை) settles the next seven (எழுமை). Restraint of the five senses (126) and learning (398) end in the identical formula எழுமையும் ஏமாப்புடைத்து, and blameless children keep evil off for seven births (62); the same reckoning runs the other way when the fool makes in one birth the mire he sinks in for seven (835) and neglect of what is praised leaves nothing through seven (538). Taken together they make a single life the lever on all later ones, for good or ill, and place sense-restraint, learning and children side by side as goods that outlast the body.
limits: This is a recurring formula in five verses, not a doctrine the book argues for. Parimelazhagar reads எழுமை as seven future births, while Kalaignar renders it as seven generations or simply all time, which removes rebirth from these verses.
audit_issue: Only 126, 398 and 835 pair ஒருமை with எழுமை; 62 (எழுபிறப்பும்) and 538 (எழுமையும்) give the seven-birth consequence without the one-birth term. 107 (எழுமை எழுபிறப்பும் உள்ளுவர்) is another எழுமை verse the thread does not mention.

title: Births: a span to secure or a cycle to end?
claim: The chapters on renunciation and true knowledge treat birth itself as the evil: craving is its seed (361) and cutting attachment cuts it off (349); delusion produces a joyless birth (351) and birth is then called a folly (358); learning that sees the real leads to the path of not returning (356), and certain knowledge makes further birth unthinkable (357), against 339's endless round of sleep and waking. Elsewhere births are a span to protect, and the two attitudes meet over learning: in 398 it protects through seven births, in 356 it ends them. Likewise 73 gives the body-bond a purpose in love, while for one set on cutting births even the body is excess (345).
limits: The verses never set the two attitudes against each other; on Parimelazhagar's reading they belong to different stages, the householder and the renouncer, so this is a shift of aim rather than a contradiction. Kalaignar reads 356 as not returning to household life, which drops rebirth from it.
audit_issue: The second attitude is thin: 398 values learning carried across births (எழுமையும் ஏமாப்பு), not births as a span to secure, and Kalaignar reads எழுமை as generations. 73 values the life-body bond as the fruit of love, which is the only real counterweight. The 'birth as evil' half is well supported; the contrast the title draws rests on two weak verses.

title: Who guards the king?
claim: Several verses across chapters 39, 45, 55 and 56 place a ruler's safety and ruin inside his own conduct rather than with enemies. Justice, which earns him the name இறை in 388, is what guards him in 547 if he practises it without fail. A king without rebukers perishes with no one to destroy him (448), and the unapproachable king who does not examine and do justice perishes by himself (548), while neglect of daily justice ruins his land day by day (553). The temperament that prevents this is the ability to bear bitter words (389), which Parimelazhagar reads as the speech of the rebuking companions of 447 and 448.
limits: The claim is about how these verses frame the king's fall; the book elsewhere treats foreign enemies and fortifications at length. Manakkudavar reads 389 differently, so the 389 links depend on Parimelazhagar.
audit_issue: 553 has the land ruined day by day, not the king perishing by himself, so it widens the claim from the ruler's safety to the realm's.

title: The sceptre as rain
claim: Chapters 55 and 56 build the king's rule onto the image of rain. People live looking to the sceptre as the world lives looking to the sky (542); the just sceptre brings rain and harvest together (545), and the bent one stops the rain (559); the king's lack of kindness is to his people what drought is to the earth (557), and when the guardian does not guard, cows yield less and the learned forget their books (560), the books whose origin 543 makes the sceptre. Read together, the verses present just rule not only as like rain but, on Parimelazhagar's reading of 545 and 559, as a cause of the actual weather.
limits: Whether the weather verses are literal is a commentators' dispute: Kalaignar turns 545 into a comparison and 559 into neglected reservoirs. 542 and 557 are explicit comparisons and do not by themselves claim moral weather.
audit_issue: The links from 390 and 528 add little: 390 only lists அளி, and 528's 'live looking to' concerns kin and the king's recognition of rank, not rain.

title: Is enmity to be shunned or sought?
claim: Chapters 86 to 88 give both answers. 871 says enmity, having no good in it, should not be wanted even in jest, and 852 and 855 praise not returning harm and leaning away from hostility. Yet 861 says to keep enmity with the weak, 867 says a certain man's enmity must be got even by paying for it, 879 says to fell the thorn tree while young, and 880 says those who do not break a foe's pride are not even alive, with 759 naming wealth as the blade for it. The same section prizes turning enmity into friendship (874), while 830 says an enemy who turns friend gets only one's face.
limits: Parimelazhagar reconciles 871 with 861 and 867 by limiting it to enmity that brings no gain (மாணாத பகை); the verses do not draw that line. Kalaignar reads 861 the other way, as fighting the strong rather than the weak, which removes one side of the conflict on his reading.
audit_issue: 874 and 830 are less opposed than the claim suggests: Parimelazhagar reads 874's turning enmity to friendship as a king's policy used when needed (வேண்டியவழி), and Manakkudavar reads it as treating enemies like friends, which is close to 830's face-only friendship. Manakkudavar narrows 867 too, saying such a foe cannot do real harm, so the conflict with 871 is eased by both commentators, not by Parimelazhagar alone.

title: The enemy inside is worse than the enemy outside
claim: Across the chapters on ministers, the land, bad friendship and inner enmity, the book ranks the hidden or intimate enemy below the open one. 639 and 817 share one construction, setting crores of open enemies against a single plotting minister or a laughing friend; 882 gives the rule (fear not the sword-like foe but the kin-like one), 828 shows the weapon hidden in folded hands, and 735 adds inner enmity (உட்பகை) to 734's outside threats to a land.
limits: Parimelazhagar reads உறும் in 639 as 'that many enemies will arise' rather than 'is better', which weakens its parallel with 817. 734-735 only lists the inner enemy beside the outer one and does not rank them.
audit_issue: 'Ranks the hidden enemy below the open one' means 'as worse than', which the wording leaves ambiguous. Chapter 89 (883, 884, 889) adds direct support the thread does not use.

title: One art of reading signs, in court and in love
claim: Chapters 71 and 110 share the title குறிப்பறிதல், and the verses apply one theory of the speaking eye and face in both books. The minister who knows the king's mind without being told (701), the eye that reads a sign by a sign (705), the face one need only stand before (708) and the eye that tells enmity and friendship (709) return in love as eyes that agree and make words useless (1100), eyes that speak against the beloved's will (1271, using the same verb உரை as 709), and the crystal image of 706 in 1273. In court the reading is a rare skill a subordinate exercises on a ruler; in love it is mutual and replaces speech.
limits: The book does not cross-refer between the chapters; the parallel rests on shared title, vocabulary and images. Parimelazhagar adds for 708 that speaking would lessen both parties, a concern for dignity the love verses do not share.
audit_issue: The love-side verses 1271 and 1273 are not mutual: the man reads a sign she hides, and in 1273 Parimelazhagar has him admit he cannot read it and ask the friend. In court the reading is not only of a ruler: in 709 Parimelazhagar's ministers read foreign kings' eyes, and in 708 the one read is a petitioner. Parimelazhagar takes 1100's வாய்ச்சொற்கள் as words not meant in the heart, so the eyes expose speech rather than simply replacing it.

title: Can signs be trusted?
claim: The face shows what is strongest in the heart (706) and gets there before the mind (707), and the love books push this further: bangles know of the lover's parting before the woman does (1277), and desire breaks out like a sneeze without intent (1253). Yet signs can be worn against the heart: deceivers smile sweetly while bitter within (824, against 706), lovers put on hostile looks while close (1097), which complicates 709's reading of enmity in the eye, and in 1312 the woman takes his sneeze, the type of the involuntary in 1253, as calculated. The book holds both that the body betrays the heart and that it can be made to lie, and leaves the reader's skill to decide.
limits: The feigned signs differ in kind: 824 is an enemy's deception, 1097 a lover's play, read with relief rather than fear. This extends the existing thread; its link 824-826 (enemies' words soon seen through) lies outside this packet and should be kept when merging, as should the note that 71 and 828 on tears do not conflict.
audit_issue: Parimelazhagar reads 1277's தணந்தமை as his mental separation while still physically with her, so the bangles detect an inner change, which strengthens the 'signs before mind' point.

title: Why the planned sulk always fails
claim: Across four chapters of the Book of Love the woman sets out to sulk and her own heart defeats the plan. 1246 predicts it (the heart's anger is false heat, since it cannot hold out once it sees him), 1259 and 1284 report it as something that happened (she went to sulk; the heart went to unite), 1260 gives the reason as a general nature (hearts like fat in fire cannot say 'we will hold out in a sulk'), and 1294 draws the consequence that she will no longer plan with her heart. Together they treat ஊடல், the sulk that a lover's art requires, as a plan the speaker's own heart reliably breaks.
limits: These are dramatised speeches of one speaker and do not claim the sulk is never kept; the man's 1310 calls his own heart's wish to join mere craving, so the pattern is not confined to the woman, but this thread rests on her verses.
audit_issue: In 1246 it is the heart's own anger, refusing to go to him over his cruelty in Parimelazhagar's frame, that she calls false. So 1246 is not her plan to sulk but the heart's pretended sulk, which still fits the pattern.

title: Whose heart belongs to whom?
claim: A complaint about the ownership of hearts runs from chapter 121 to the close of chapter 130. 1204 asks whether she has a place in his heart since he is always in hers; 1205 answers that he bars her from his heart yet keeps entering hers, and 1243 takes his lack of pitying thought as settled. 1291 turns the same imbalance inward: his heart stays his, so why is hers not hers? 1299 and 1300 generalise it (when one's own heart is no companion or kin, no stranger can be), and Parimelazhagar gives these two to the man, so the chapter ends with the complaint voiced from the other side.
limits: Pope reads 1205 the other way (he has imprisoned her in his heart), and Manakkudavar gives 1299 to the woman, which removes the two-sided ending. Elsewhere his dwelling in her heart is something she cherishes, not a grievance (1128, 1218, 1249).

title: A life judged by what remains of it
claim: Several verses measure a life by what is left after it (எச்சம்) and make renown that remainder: 238 calls it a disgrace to leave no legacy of renown, 1004 asks what the unwanted hoarder imagines will remain of him, and 233 says nothing but renown stands undying. The same logic reaches death in war: 777's warrior wants fame more than life, and 235, as Parimelazhagar glosses it, explains a death that is existence through the body of fame outliving the body of flesh; 970 shows the world praising those who choose death over disgrace, as 240 says a life without renown is no life.
limits: The word எச்சம் is read differently: Parimelazhagar takes it as offspring in 114 but as surviving renown in 1004, so 114 belongs to the thread only on the Kalaignar-style reading. The link from 235 to the warrior depends on Parimelazhagar's gloss of a compressed verse.
audit_issue: 970 is in the chapter on honour (மானம்): what it describes is refusing to live under disgrace and being praised for it, so it says nothing directly about fame outliving the body. The war-death strand depends on Parimelazhagar's gloss of 235 and also on reading 970 through 235.

title: Many roads to renown, and one it may not take
claim: The book names renown as the reward of different virtues: giving (231, 232), not lying (296, 'no renown like it'), forbearance (156) and dropping hostility (853, renown on Parimelazhagar's reading), and dying in battle (777, set beside giving in 231). 232 and 296 both speak as if naming the chief source, though Parimelazhagar narrows 296 to the cause of renown in this life. Then the Book of Wealth limits renown as a motive: 652 makes it one test of an act, but 962 says those who want honour will not do the unworthy even for renown, taking up the case 653 leaves open.
limits: The superlatives may be rhetorical rather than a ranking (compare thread:competing_supremes). 652 pairs renown with good (or, for Parimelazhagar, with virtue hereafter), so it never made renown alone sufficient; 962 sharpens rather than reverses it.
audit_issue: Parimelazhagar sends several of these roads back through giving: he grounds 233's unmatched renown in giving life, limbs and goods, and 853's renown in friends, wealth and then கொடை. On his reading the sources converge more than the claim suggests.

title: Honour as virtue and as fault
claim: The same word மானம் is required of the king, paired with valour (384), and of the army (766), and chapter 97 ranks it above even what is indispensable (961, which Parimelazhagar reads as life itself). Yet 432 lists மாண்பிறந்த மானம், honour that has passed beyond the fine, among a ruler's faults, and 1028 says the one raising his family ruins it if he idles and minds his மானம். The book marks the line between the virtue and the fault by a qualifier or by context, not by a separate word, so the term cannot be read as uniformly praised.
limits: Commentators fill the boundary differently: Parimelazhagar makes 432's fault refusing to bow to elders and forcing through what was resolved, and 1028's a resentment at suffering for the family's sake, while Kalaignar reads 1028 as being shaken by insult. On those readings 961 and 1028 do not strictly conflict.
audit_issue: 961 does not use the word மானம்; its place in the honour chapter and Parimelazhagar's gloss (lowering of one's birth) supply the link. 384's மானம் is also qualified (மறனிழுக்கா), so qualifiers mark the virtue as well as the fault.

title: What is worth more than staying alive?
claim: Four chapters rank continued life below another value in the same form: one gives up life rather than honour (969, 968, 970), rather than shame (1017), or to keep a vow in battle (779). 971 turns the ranking into a definition: disgrace is saying 'we will live without it'. Parimelazhagar gives the shared reason at 969: the body passes and honour lasts. Read together, these verses make 'choosing to live on' itself the mark of the lesser person across civil, military and inner virtue.
limits: 971's 'it' is aspiration (Parimelazhagar's ஊக்கம்), not honour, and 779 concerns a soldier's vow. In the Book of Love 1132 sets shame aside to save life (see thread:love_overturns), and 963 and 988 answer shrunken circumstances with bearing, not death.
audit_issue: Parimelazhagar ties 968's பெருந்தகைமை to the honour that comes with high birth (உயர்குடிப் பிறப்பு), so on his reading part of this ranking belongs to the well-born rather than to everyone.

title: Who gives the secret away?
claim: Although chapter 115 is about the town's gossip, verses across chapters 114, 116, 118, 124 and 126 locate the leak in the lover herself: her love reels through the street (1139), her eyes are beaten drums that make her secret easy to learn (1180), slipping bangles and wasted shoulders announce his leaving (1157, 1233, 1235), and the same line, மறையிறந்து மன்று படும், is said of love in general (1138) and then of herself after she thought herself firm (1254). Together they make the town's talk downstream of what her own body publishes.
limits: Most of these are framed as 'seems to' (போலும்) or rhetorical questions, and Parimelazhagar gives 1233 and 1235 to the friend (Manakkudavar gives 1233 to the woman). The thread does not claim she wishes the secret known.
audit_issue: Both commentators read 1157's bangles as telling the woman or her friend of his leaving (Parimelazhagar: உனக்கு அறிவியாவோ; Manakkudavar: எமக்கு அறிவியாவோ), not as broadcasting it to the town. 1139 has her love, not her body, reeling through the street.

title: Should the absent lover be blamed?
claim: Several speeches have the woman rebut the town's verdict that he is loveless or has left her, by appeal to a presence it cannot see: in her unblinking eye (1129), her heart (1130) and her dreams (1219, 1220); Parimelazhagar frames 1129 and 1219 as replies to the friend's blaming him. But 1188 complains the opposite, that people talk only of her pallor and no one says he left her, and 1190 then accepts that name if only his unkindness is not spread. The friend's voice in 1232 and 1235 (on Parimelazhagar's assignment) says her body itself reports his unkindness. The book keeps her divided between wanting his fault named and shielding him from it.
limits: These are dramatised speeches in different situations, and 1188's 'no one' and 1220's townspeople need not be the same audience. On Parimelazhagar's reading the laughers of 1140 are the friend's teasing, not the town.
audit_issue: The 'wanting his fault named' side rests on 1188 alone, and this edition has no Parimelazhagar or Manakkudavar gloss for that verse, so its reading follows Pope and Kalaignar. In 1190 Parimelazhagar's தூற்றார் are நட்டோர, close friends, not the town.
